title: Non-signaling assistance in prepare-and-measure scenarios with classical communication
authors: José Nogueira, Carlos Vieira, Lucas E. A. Porto, Lucas Pollyceno, Rafael Rabelo, Otfried Gühne
abstract: Extracting the full power of non-local correlations in prepare-and-measure (PM) scenarios requires precise control over the timing and structure of the receiver's measurements. Indeed, recent developments in entanglement-assisted classical communication scenarios have shown that adaptive strategies-where the receiver uses the transmitted message to guide their measurement choice-can outperform standard non-adaptive protocols. Moving beyond quantum theory, however, the ultimate limits of such advantages remain largely unexplored. In this work, we thoroughly study adaptive and non-adaptive non-signaling (NS) assistance in PM scenarios with classical communication. We provide simple characterizations of the sets of behaviors that can be realized using both non-adaptive and adaptive NS assistance in arbitrary PM scenarios. As a consequence, we show that non-adaptive NS assistance is already strong enough to reproduce quantum communication with the same message dimension: the transmission of a qudit can be simulated by a classical dit assisted non-adaptively by NS correlations. We then compare adaptive and non-adaptive NS assistance. We prove that any adaptive NS advantage can be traced back to scenarios in which the receiver has no measurement choice, ruling out the genuinely multi-setting advantages found in entanglement-assisted quantum protocols. Finally, we identify all PM scenarios where adaptive NS strategies provide a strict advantage over non-adaptive ones.
summary: The paper provides a detailed comparison between adaptive and non-adaptive Non-Signaling (NS) assistance in Prepare-and-Measure communication models. It establishes that while NS assistance can simulate quantum qudit transmission classically, any genuine advantage gained by adaptivity over non-adaptivity is restricted to highly specific scenarios. The findings help delineate the true power of different types of non-local correlations.
main_problem: The paper investigates the operational advantage of using adaptive versus non-adaptive Non-Signaling (NS) assistance in Prepare-and-Measure (PM) quantum communication scenarios.
main_result: It proves that any genuine adaptive advantage over non-adaptive NS assistance can be traced back to scenarios where the receiver has no measurement choice, thus ruling out genuinely multi-setting advantages found in entanglement-assisted protocols.
method: The authors characterize the sets of achievable correlations by deriving necessary and sufficient conditions based on input-discrimination inequalities derived from structural properties of non-signaling boxes.
model_or_system: The model is a Prepare-and-Measure (PM) scenario $(n_X; n_Y, n_B)$, where Alice prepares a message $a$ based on input $x$, and Bob measures using input $y$ to produce output $b$. The analysis compares correlations achievable with classical communication, non-adaptive NS assistance ($	ext{NSNA}$), and adaptive NS assistance ($	ext{NSA}$).
key_observables: The set of achievable correlation functions $q(b|x, y)$, and the maximum discrimination score $\max_{x \in [n_X]} q(b|x, y)$.
important_parameters: Message dimension ($n_A$), input sizes ($n_X, n_Y$), and output size ($n_B$). The comparison hinges on whether $n_A$ is large relative to these dimensions.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies heavily on reducing the general PM scenario characterization to fixed-$y$ sub-behaviors (Theorem 3) and comparing structural constraints derived from NS boxes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the basic PM setup. Other figures detail the mathematical structures for non-adaptive and adaptive NS assistance, showing how inputs $x, y$ lead to an intermediate shared resource $\alpha eta$ or a message $a$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the general framework of achievable correlations using various resources (classical, EA, NS). It then focuses on characterizing non-adaptive ($	ext{NSNA}$) and adaptive ($	ext{NSA}$) NS assistance separately. The core is comparing these two sets to pinpoint exactly when $	ext{NSA}$ provides a strict advantage over $	ext{NSNA}$.
why_interesting: This work rigorously quantifies the limits of communication protocols using non-local correlations, providing fundamental boundaries for what can be achieved with limited resources like classical messages and NS assistance, which is crucial for understanding device-independent quantum information tasks.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of a prepare-and-measure scenario. Alice en- codes her input x into a preparation device, which emits either a classical or quantum system sent to Bob. Bob receives the system, chooses an input y for his measurement device, and produces an output b. The devices may share correlations, which can be clas- sical (shared randomness λ) or quantum (arising from a shared entangled state ρAB).

FIG. 2. Schematic representation of a prepare-and-measure sce- nario with non-adaptive non-signaling assistance, according to the definition in Eq. (6). Alice and Bob share an arbitrary non- signaling box in the Bell scenario (nX, nA; nY , nβ). Alice inputs x into her share of the box, obtains outcome a, and communicates it to Bob. Bob independently inputs y into his share of the box and obtains β. Finally, he post-processes a,β to produce the output b.

FIG. 3. Schematic representation of a prepare-and-measure sce- nario with adaptive non-signaling assistance, according to Eq. (8). Alice and Bob share an arbitrary non-signaling box in the Bell sce- nario (nX, nA; nY nA, nB). Alice inputs x into her share of the box, obtains outcome a, and communicates it to Bob. Bob then inputs the composite setting (y, a) into his share of the box and obtains the output b. The protocol is adaptive because Bob’s input to the shared box depends on the message received from Alice.
